Lessons.Title: Interpreting Exponential Functions
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: interpret exponential function notation, choose a reasonable real-world domain and range, represent an exponential relationship with discrete points or a continuous curve according to modeling assumptions, and compare growth/decay with other functions. First-party Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 5 Lesson 9, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/5/9/preparation.html and student tasks https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/students/1/5/9/index.html (CC BY 4.0). The source includes a solar-cost graph and x² versus2^x reasoning.

Independent hypothetical technology-component price model: P(t)=100(0.8)^t dollars for t≥0 years after purchase. It has initial $100, decay factor0.8 and positive decreasing outputs. On a continuous-time modeling assumption domain is [0,∞) and range (0,100] dollars; if only whole-year snapshots are recorded, represent discrete t=0,1,2,... and their specific outputs rather than a proven continuous process.

For t0,1,2,3, costs are100,80,64,51.20 dollars. P(2)=64 means a modelled price of $64 two years after baseline, not an observed sale receipt. For all finite t≥0, model output remains positive, so y=0 is an asymptote rather than attained value.
Compare expressions x² and2^x: at x2 both equal4, x4 both equal16, but at x3 they give9 and8. They are not equivalent functions, even if some inputs produce equal outputs.

Student task: graph with a labelled time domain, interpret P(2), identify which points could belong, compare with an integer-only representation, and produce a counterexample to equation equivalence. Teacher-scored rubric0–2 each for notation, graph/domain, range/asymptote, and reasoned comparison.

KeyConcepts.Title: Function context
KeyConcepts.Definition: P(t) is the modeled output at time t.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Do not confuse prediction with empirical measurement.

KeyConcepts.Title: Exponential domain and range
KeyConcepts.Definition: For positive initial value and0<b<1 on t≥0, outputs lie in (0,a].
KeyConcepts.Rule: Specify discrete or continuous time assumption.

KeyConcepts.Title: Non-equivalent formulas
KeyConcepts.Definition: Two expressions can agree at particular inputs but differ as functions.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Test enough inputs to disprove universal identity.

WorkedExamples.Title: Describe domain and range
WorkedExamples.Question: Assume continuous real time t≥0 for P(t).
WorkedExamples.Method: Derive the specific first-party mathematical rule, independently verify it and interpret with the stated domains.
Steps: As time increases, factor0.8^t remains positive and decreases.
WorkedExamples.Check: Zero is approached but never reached.

WorkedExamples.Title: Disprove x²=2^x universally
WorkedExamples.Question: Check x2, x3, x4.
WorkedExamples.Method: Derive the specific first-party mathematical rule, independently verify it and interpret with the stated domains.
Steps: One counterexample suffices to show formulas not equivalent.
At4 they agree again at16, which does not repair disagreement at3.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Including zero in range of a positive decay expression at finite time
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Exponential positive base never produces exactly zero.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Equating functions because two sample points coincide
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Equality at selected inputs is not identity.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claiming model price is real market data

SummaryPoints: Interpreting notation requires units, input domain and model assumptions.
A positive decaying exponential approaches zero without attaining it.
Discrete observations and continuous curves represent different evidence levels.
Teacher scores graph/domain and counterexample explanation.
